The Red salamander (Pseudotriton ruber) is a relatively large-bodied plethodontid found in headwater streams across the eastern United States, and its physiological attributes reflect the cool, well-oxygenated aquatic environments it inhabits. Recent respirometry trials conducted at a standard experimental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] have documented a resting metabolic rate of 0.0039 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0039 milliliters of oxygen per hour] for this species. This oxygen consumption value is modest, consistent with the generally low metabolic demands of lungless salamanders that rely entirely on cutaneous respiration. The measurement was obtained from adults in a post-absorptive state and serves as a reliable baseline for comparing the energetic costs of activity, digestion, and reproduction across the genus Pseudotriton. Such low basal rates are typical of stream-dwelling plethodontids, which experience relatively stable thermal regimes and do not require high metabolic throughput for thermoregulation.

Females of Pseudotriton ruber exhibit a distinct seasonal reproductive cycle, with oviposition occurring in late autumn or early winter following a period of gametogenesis. The maximum observed reproductive rate for this species has been characterized under controlled thermal conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], where females deposit approximately 29 to 130 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 29 to 130 eggs per year]. This range, which is expressed as total annual fecundity, reflects the substantial variation in clutch size linked to female body condition and local resource availability. The eggs are typically deposited in concealed locations within submerged stream banks or beneath large cobbles, where they undergo a prolonged incubation. The relatively high upper end of this fecundity estimate suggests that in favorable years, females may produce multiple clutches or a single very large clutch, though direct field confirmation of double-clutching remains limited.

Neonatal body size in Pseudotriton ruber is strikingly small, a feature that imposes considerable constraints on the early life stages. Newly emerged hatchlings possess a wet weight of only 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a diminutive mass that corresponds to a spherical egg diameter of roughly 3 millimeters. This tiny initial size means that the aquatic larvae are highly vulnerable to predation and desiccation during their first weeks of development, and they must begin exogenous feeding almost immediately after yolk-sac resorption. In contrast, adults of this species attain a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 10.8 grams [Wwi = 10.8 grams], representing a more than seven-hundred-fold increase in body mass from birth. This dramatic ontogenetic trajectory is supported by a prolonged larval period and a diet that shifts from small aquatic invertebrates to larger terrestrial prey following metamorphosis.

The embryonic development of Pseudotriton ruber is closely tied to water temperature, and under the cool conditions typical of its spring-fed stream habitats, the incubation period is notably extended. At a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the age at hatching, defined as the interval from oviposition to chorion rupture, spans approximately 75 days [ab = approximately 75 days]. This protracted development is a direct consequence of the slowed metabolic and enzymatic reaction rates at lower thermal regimes, a common pattern among montane and headwater-stream amphibians. The yolk-dependent larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during this entire 75-day period, with mouthparts not fully functional until after eclosion from the jelly capsule. Once hatched, the free-swimming tadpoles begin filtering organic particles from the water column, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth that will eventually lead to metamorphosis.

Longevity and the timing of reproductive maturation are key parameters shaping the life history strategy of Pseudotriton ruber, and available mark-recapture data provide valuable insights into these demographic traits. At a seasonal average temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum lifespan for this species has been estimated at approximately 20.1 years [am = approximately 20.1 years], a remarkably extended duration for a salamander of this body size and one that places it among the longer-lived members of the Plethodontidae.
